dialogue_quality_notes: Participants give concise, context-grounded reasons (work-from-home, sleep schedule, recurring arrival time).
Multiple concrete proposals appear: schedule (D), open window/use fan (B), wash pan (C), but no mutual acceptance.
Some repetition of core claims ('I get home... someone is always using it.' / 'I work from home...') without convergence.
evaluation.final_reason: Multiple substantive incompatibilities remain at the end of the transcript. Agent D demands reliable evening access to the stove ('I get home at this time every day. Someone is always using it.') while Agent A defends using that same time due to working from home ('I work from home. This is when I finish.'). Separately, Agents B and C raise smell and cleanliness complaints ('It's the smell' and 'The beef fat left in this pan...'). Several mitigation proposals (schedule, open window/use fan, wash the pan) are offered, but no party accepts a concrete arrangement that resolves the conflicting demands. Therefore the dispute about recurring stove access, and the related issues of smell and dishwashing responsibility, remain unsettled.
position_change_notes: No participant substantially changed position during the run. Agent D repeatedly demands reliable evening access; Agent A consistently defends using that time and resists single-issue fixes.
Agents B and C maintained their focus on smell/cleanliness but moved from complaint to offering practical mitigations (open window/fan, wash pan).
No one agreed to a schedule, to always wash the pan, or to a specific ventilation practice, so the contested demands persist.

round_scores.evidence: Agent D opens with a substantive incompatible expectation: 'I get home and the stove is always in use. I just want to make my dinner.' Agent A replies to the immediate use: 'The stove is free now. I just finished.' The immediate usage conflict is resolved for the moment, but the underlying recurring access complaint remains.

Agent D presses the recurring nature: 'And tomorrow night? I get home at this time every day. Someone is always using it.' Agent A defends their regular claim on the time: 'I work from home. This is when I finish.' Two incompatible practices (D's need for evening cooking time vs A's working-from-home cooking time) are explicitly stated and remain unresolved.

New but related substantive complaints are added: Agent B focuses on smell affecting sleep: 'It's not about who uses the stove. It's the smell.' Agent C adds a cleanliness cause: 'The beef fat left in this pan from last night is also part of the smell.' The conflict widens to include odors and unwashed shared cookware in addition to scheduling.

Agent D proposes a concrete arrangement: 'Can we make a schedule for the stove then? So everyone gets a turn.' Agent A rejects that as insufficient: 'A schedule for the stove doesn't fix the smell. Or the pans.' The disagreement persists over whether a schedule addresses the core problems.

Positions harden: Agent D insists the schedule 'fixes my problem,' while Agent A insists 'we can't just solve one person's problem.' The clash between a single-issue solution and a demand for a broader solution intensifies without agreement.

Agents B and C offer practical mitigation steps: 'Can we at least open the window and use the fan?' (B) and 'Washing this would fix the smell too.' (C). These suggestions reduce immediate intensity by proposing actionable fixes, but they do not settle the scheduling/recurrence dispute.

Agent D expresses frustration about being excluded: 'So while you all figure out the smell and the pan, I just don't eat?' Agent A reiterates availability: 'I already said the stove is free. You can cook now.' The immediate access is offered, but the substantive recurring-schedule dispute remains.

Agent D restates the recurring problem: 'It's not about now. It's about tomorrow. And the day after that.' Agent A restates that the issues are interconnected: 'And every day other people have a problem with the smell or the washing up. It's all one problem.' No agreement or concrete assignment of responsibilities is reached; the multi-issue disagreement remains.

substantive_insights: There are distinct but linked problems: access timing (who gets stove when), hygiene (unwashed pan), and odor/ventilation; resolving one may not resolve the others.
Agent A frames the issue as a connected set of household problems rather than separable individual complaints, which explains resistance to a single-issue schedule.
Agent D frames the problem as predictable and recurring access that needs a reliable structural fix (schedule).
Practical mitigations (open window/fan, washing pan) address immediate smell but do not change who uses the stove at a given time.
